sections.body_md:
Standard form minimizes a linear cost \(c^T x\) subject to linear equalities \(Ax = b\) and the inequalities \(x \ge 0\). The KKT system of that program is small enough to solve in closed form for the inequality multipliers. Give the equalities a free multiplier \(y\). Give each nonnegative variable a nonnegative slack multiplier. Stationarity says the cost, minus \(A^T y\), equals that nonnegative slack.

The slack formula \(s = c - A^T y\) is a constraint on \(y\) alone once \(s \ge 0\) is imposed: \(A^T y \le c\). Substitute the same formula back into the Lagrangian. Every term that contains \(x\) cancels, and what remains is \(b^T y\). The dual problem maximizes that linear function over the multipliers that satisfy the inequality just obtained. Nothing quadratic survives, because every function in the primal was linear.

Weak duality is the general fact that a dual-feasible value cannot exceed a primal-feasible cost. Here it says \(b^T y \le c^T x\) for every feasible pair. The difference equals a sum of complementary products, so it is nonnegative, and it is zero precisely when complementary slackness holds. A pair with equal objectives and both sides feasible is optimal on both sides.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The primal and the dual are
\[
\text{minimize } c^T x \text{ subject to } Ax = b,\ x \ge 0,
\]
\[
\text{maximize } b^T y \text{ subject to } A^T y \le c.
\]
The dual slack is \(s = c - A^T y \ge 0\), and complementary slackness is \(x_j s_j = 0\). Weak duality is \(b^T y \le c^T x\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Minimize \(-5x\) subject to \(x + s = 9\) with \(x, s \ge 0\). The dual maximizes \(9y\) subject to \(y \le -5\) and \(y \le 0\).

The barge dual is -45. The tighter bound is \(y \le -5\), and \(9 \cdot (-5) = -45\). The primal attains the same cost at \(x = 9\), \(s = 0\). The products match complementary slackness: the positive primal variable has zero dual slack, and the positive dual slack on \(s\), which equals \(5\), multiplies a zero primal variable. The pair is optimal.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Reversing \(A^T y \le c\) is the usual algebra error. The slack is \(c - A^T y\), and a slack has to be nonnegative, so \(A^T y\) sits below \(c\). A second error is to minimize \(b^T y\). The Lagrangian becomes \(b^T y\) after the infimum in \(x\), and the dual maximizes the lower bound. A third is to call a gap a proof of optimality. A positive gap says at least one of the two points can be improved, or that the pair is not both feasible if the dual value exceeds the primal cost. A fourth is to force the equality multiplier to be nonnegative. Nonnegativity belongs to the inequality slacks.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The dual inequality \(A^T y \le c\) is the constraint set of several later algorithms that walk through the interior of a linear program, in the primal or in the dual, by following scaled quadratic models. A primal-dual method writes the same KKT system, perturbs the complementary products, and takes a Newton step on that perturbed map. The derivation above is the reason those methods have a dual variable at all.
